description: Solo developer working on NASA Space Apps 2026: “Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions.” Skilled in Python, Django, DRF, React, Next.js, PostgreSQL, Pandas, NumPy, Scikit-learn, data visualization, and REST APIs. I aim to build a practical AI-powered health monitoring prototype for astronauts during long-duration space missions.
summary: AstroHealth Monitor is an educational web dashboard that turns NASA astronaut blood data into clear, easy-to-read health indicators. Long space missions affect muscle and bone, the cardiovascular system, sleep, radiation exposure and psychological stress. Using NASA OSDR Inspiration4 data (4 astronauts, 28 samples), we compare each astronaut with their own pre-flight baseline. Right after return, inflammation and immune markers shifted in the same direction in all four astronauts (for example IL-6 about +90%). Users can enter sample measurements, view trends, receive colour-coded warnings based on lab reference ranges and clearly explained illustrative thresholds, and read educational prevention tips. The project shows how space research data can support astronaut wellbeing monitoring on long-duration missions. It is a research and educational prototype, not a clinically validated diagnostic tool, and it does not diagnose or predict disease.
details:
PROBLEM

Astronauts on long missions face muscle and bone loss, cardiovascular changes, sleep disruption and fatigue, radiation exposure and psychological stress. Monitoring data is complex, so we built a simple tool that explains it.

WHAT IT DOES

AstroHealth Monitor is a Streamlit web app with seven pages:

1. Overview: five health-area cards (muscle and bone, cardiovascular, sleep, radiation, psychological stress) and the biggest changes found in NASA data.

2. Enter measurements: users type sample blood values and indicators such as sleep, heart rate, radiation dose, stress, bone and muscle change.

3. Trends and indicators: per-astronaut trend lines over seven timepoints with lab reference ranges, plus a heatmap of change from each astronaut's own baseline.

4. Risk indicators: colour-coded warnings (Within range, Watch, Attention) with the rules explained in plain language.

5. Recommendations: educational prevention measures for each health area.

6. NASA research and data: the datasets used, model results and references.

7. About and limits: methods and limitations.

HOW IT WORKS

We used NASA OSDR Inspiration4 datasets (OSD-569 and OSD-575): complete blood count, comprehensive metabolic panel, and immune and cardiovascular panels, for 4 astronauts at 7 timepoints (28 samples). In Python (Google Colab) we merged and cleaned the data, corrected a suspect platelet value, converted CRP units, and compared every astronaut with their own pre-flight baseline using z-scores. Right after return (R+1), inflammation and immune markers moved in the same direction in all four astronauts (IL-6 about +90%, MCP-1 about +97%, monocytes about +26%, white blood cells about -15%). A regularised model with leave-one-astronaut-out validation separated post-return from pre-flight samples better than chance (balanced accuracy 0.83, AUC 0.96, permutation p = 0.025). This is a small-sample pattern, not a predictor. Warnings in the app use laboratory reference ranges from the NASA data plus clearly labelled illustrative thresholds.

IMPACT

The tool shows how open space-research data can be turned into understandable health indicators and educational guidance, supporting future long-duration mission monitoring and public science education.

TOOLS

Python, pandas, scikit-learn, matplotlib, Streamlit, Google Colab, GitHub.

SOURCE CODE

GitHub: https://github.com/muhammadmateensadiq/astrohealth-monitor

LIMITATIONS

Only 4 astronauts and 28 samples from a short (about 3-day) commercial mission. Long-duration effects such as bone loss are explained from NASA research, not measured here. Thresholds for sleep, heart rate, radiation, stress, bone and muscle are illustrative. The source data contains two different lab reference sets. This is a research and educational prototype, not a clinically validated tool. It does not diagnose or predict disease.

TEAM

MMS : Muhammad Mateen Sadiq
